name: Infectious disease specialists
summary: How expats access infectious disease (ID) physicians in Singapore for complex infections, fever of unknown origin, tropical exposures, HIV care, and post-travel syndromes beyond a standard GP or travel-vaccine visit.
body:
Travel clinics handle vaccines and malaria tablets. Infectious disease specialists handle the harder cases: prolonged fever, recurrent infections, imported tropical disease, antibiotic-resistant organisms, HIV, and infections in immunocompromised patients.

## When ID (not just GP) makes sense
- Fever lasting beyond a simple viral window, especially after travel
- Recurrent UTIs, skin infections, or osteomyelitis needing stewardship
- Positive blood cultures or hospital-acquired infection follow-up
- HIV diagnosis, PrEP complexity, or opportunistic infection workup
- Parasitic or tropical disease suspicion (dengue complications, melioidosis risk after soil/flood exposure, etc.)

Public hospital ID departments run consult services and specialty clinics. Private ID physicians exist in major medical centres and are useful when you need rapid outpatient workup before a flight home or school term starts.

## Dengue and tropical living
Singapore's dengue clusters mean many febrile illnesses start with a GP NS1/Ig test. Complicated dengue, warning signs, or diagnostic uncertainty after negative early tests may still need hospital pathways. Flood or construction-site soil exposure raises different differentials — tell the clinician exactly where you were.

## Antimicrobial stewardship
Expat habits of “just in case” antibiotics from home cabinets collide with Singapore stewardship culture. Bring culture results rather than demanding a broad-spectrum script. If you arrived mid-course on an overseas antibiotic, show the drug name and day count.

## How to choose
Prefer ID physicians affiliated with hospitals that can escalate imaging, bronchoscopy, or inpatient isolation quickly. For HIV and sexual-health continuity, ask about confidentiality practices and long-term refill logistics on your pass type. Pair travel-vaccine planning with a separate travel clinic when you only need shots — do not consume ID slots for routine Yellow Fever paperwork.

## Practical tip
After regional travel, keep a simple exposure log (dates, countries, freshwater, insect bites, new sexual contacts, animal scratches). ID consults go faster with that timeline than with “I felt sick sometime after the trip.”
whenToEngage: When fever or infection is prolonged, travel-related, recurrent, antibiotic-resistant, HIV-related, or too complex for GP-only management — especially after tropical exposure or hospital discharge.
